transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit hard to explain without sounding completely vain, but I'm just having a really hard time lately with... well, my face. Specifically, the lower half of it. What brings me in is that I just keep getting completely stuck on this sagging, uneven look right around my jawline and really just down the whole one side of my face. It's like the skin is just pulling down differently on that side, making me look totally lopsided. 

It really started bothering me—I mean, taking up a lot of my mental energy—after we got these family photos back recently. We had this big get-together, and my wife hired a professional photographer, and when I saw the digital proofs... I mean, I don't know if it was the lighting or the lenses they use, but I just couldn't look at anything else. I zoomed right in on my face, and it was just glaringly obvious to me how droopy that side of my jaw is. I must have spent hours just staring at those pictures on my computer, comparing different angles, looking at the shadows. 

And the incredibly frustrating part is, I try to talk to my wife about it, you know, just to see if she thinks I should look into doing something about it, and she just completely waves it off. She says she barely notices anything at all. Which, you know, she's my wife, she's probably just trying to be nice, but even at work it's the same thing. I'm a personal financial advisor, so I sit across a desk from clients all day, face-to-face, talking about their life savings. Trust and presentation are huge in my line of work; I need to look sharp and put-together. I've actually kind of fished for comments a few times, or sort of apologized for looking a bit worn out or off, and my clients just look at me blankly like they have absolutely no idea what I'm talking about. They say they don't see it. But I know it's there. I see it every single morning in the mirror, and it's just really distracting me from everything else I'm supposed to be focusing on.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of your jawline being uneven is not entirely accurate?

Well, I mean... I suppose anything is possible, right? Logically, I know that if my wife says she doesn't see it, and my clients—who look at me for hours while we go over their portfolios—say they don't see it, then maybe it's not as glaring as I think. But... it's just so hard to accept that when I can see it so clearly myself. 

I mean, like I said, it really all comes back to those family photos. I just keep getting stuck on it. I look in the mirror, and my eyes just immediately go to that sagging, uneven look right around my jawline, and down that whole one side of my face. It's like a magnet. And I try to tell myself, "Okay, maybe it's just the lighting in the bathroom," so I'll go check in the hallway mirror, or I'll use the reflection in my phone screen when it's dark, or I'll pull up those digital proofs from the photographer again... and it's always there. 

So, to answer your question, do I think my perception could be inaccurate? Maybe a little? Maybe I'm hyper-focusing? But it feels so real to me. It's not like I'm imagining the skin itself—it's right there. And it's just so frustrating when everyone else acts like I'm crazy or fishing for compliments when I bring it up. I just want to look normal, you know? Symmetrical. Professional. And right now, I just feel like this one side of my face is dragging my whole appearance down, regardless of what anyone else claims they do or don't see.
Is your concern about your jawline affecting your ability to focus on your work or daily activities?

Well, yes and no, I suppose. I mean, I'm still getting through my work, obviously. I have to. My clients depend on me, and in the financial sector, you can't just drop the ball because you're having a bad day. So, I am still doing the job, running the numbers, making the calls. But... it's definitely bleeding into things. 

Like, the mornings have become this whole ordeal. I used to just shower, shave, throw on a suit, and be out the door. Now, I'm spending so much time in front of the mirror, trying to shave in a way that maybe creates a shadow to hide the droop, or adjusting my collar, or just... staring. I've been running late, getting out the door slower, which means I'm rushing to client meetings, and that's not like me at all. I pride myself on being early. 

And then, during the actual appointments... I'm there physically, but mentally, I catch myself drifting. I'll be sitting across from a couple discussing their retirement portfolio, and instead of being fully present, I'm suddenly hyper-aware of the angle of my head. I'll catch my reflection in the window or a framed picture on my desk, and my train of thought just derails. I start wondering if they're staring at my jaw, if they think I look old or tired, or if they're questioning my competence because I look lopsided. I'm just less present. It takes so much energy to pull my focus back to the spreadsheets.

And it's not just work, either. Outside the office, it's starting to dictate what I do. My wife and I usually love going to these local gallery events—we have a few friends in the local art scene—but I've actually skipped the last few art openings. I just made up some excuse about being tired from work, but the truth is, I just couldn't stomach the idea of being in those bright, overhead gallery lights. And there are always people taking pictures at those things for social media or whatever, and I just... I didn't want to be seen. I couldn't handle the thought of ending up in the background of someone's photo, completely unprepared, with my face looking the way it does. So, yeah, I'm still functioning, but it's like this constant, heavy static in the background of everything I'm trying to do.
Has your concern about your jawline affected your relationships with friends or family members?

No, I wouldn't say it's really caused any problems there. I mean, not actual problems with the relationships themselves. My wife, for instance—like I mentioned before, she just kind of brushes it off. We've been married for fifteen years, and she's incredibly patient. We aren't getting into, you know, arguments about my jawline or anything dramatic like that. It's more just... a routine now. I'll be by the bathroom mirror, maybe adjusting my tie, and I'll ask her, "Hey, does the left side look a little heavier today? Does it look like it's pulling down more than yesterday?" And she'll just be doing her makeup or putting on her earrings and she'll say, "You look fine, stop worrying about it." So there's no real friction. I think she just doesn't know what else to say, or maybe she really just doesn't see it, but it certainly hasn't hurt our marriage. 

And with friends... well, it's pretty much the same story. Like I was saying about those gallery events I've been skipping. We have this couple we're close with, Mark and Elena—they're the ones heavily involved in the local art scene, Mark actually does some really incredible mixed-media stuff—and usually, we're the first ones on their invite list. When I bailed on the last two openings, Mark did text me. But he wasn't mad. He was just checking in, asking if everything was okay at the firm, if I was working too many late nights. I just told him it was the end-of-quarter rush, you know, portfolio rebalancing and all that, and I was just totally wiped out. He completely bought it. We still text about the game, we're supposed to get a round of golf in next month, so the friendship itself is totally fine. 

So, no, nobody is upset with me, and I haven't had any falling out with anyone over this. It's not like I'm completely isolating myself from the world or snapping at my family. It's just... it's more of an internal distraction. I just keep the real reason to myself. So, yeah, I'd say my relationships are perfectly intact. It's really just my own comfort level when I'm around them that's the issue, not the relationships themselves. If anything, I'm probably just a little quieter when we do go out, but nobody seems to have noticed that either.
Are you avoiding social interactions because of your concerns about your jawline?

Well, yeah, I guess that goes right back to what I was just talking about with Mark and Elena and those gallery events. So, yes, I suppose I am avoiding some things. It is not like I am a total hermit or anything. I mean, I still get through my work, I still go into the office every day because, well, I have to. But, like I mentioned, I have been so much slower getting out the door in the mornings for my client meetings because I am just stuck in front of the mirror trying to make it look right. And then during those actual appointments, I am just less present. I am sitting there running the numbers, but my mind is completely focused on how my face looks from across the desk instead of the client in front of me. 

But as for purely social interactions, yeah, skipping those art openings is definitely because of this. I just really did not want to be seen. And it is the photographs, especially. At those events, everyone always has their phones out, they are constantly taking pictures for social media or the gallery newsletter or whatever, and the thought of being caught off guard in one of those photos, with my jaw looking all uneven and sagging... I just cannot handle it. It is so much easier to just stay home and tell them I am exhausted from work than to go out and spend the entire evening dodging cameras and trying to find the dimmest lighting in the room. So, even though I am still functioning and doing the mandatory stuff, if there is a social event where I might be photographed or really looked at, I am definitely starting to avoid it.
Do you think there's any possibility that the unevenness you see in your jawline isn't actually there?

I mean... I hear what you're asking. And logically, I try to tell myself that. I really do. Because, you know, that's actually the whole reason I finally decided to come in and talk to someone about this. What brings me in is that I just keep getting completely stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and on that one side of my face. It all really started—or at least got so much worse—after I was looking through all these family photos. We had a big get-together a while back, and when the digital album got sent around, I was just scrolling through, and it hit me like a ton of bricks. In every single picture, I just looked so lopsided. The whole side of my jaw just looked like it was pulling down, just drooping. 

But then, you know, I ask my wife about it, like I mentioned earlier, and she just brushes it off. She says she barely notices anything at all. And even at work, I'll try to subtly fish for comments from clients, maybe make a self-deprecating joke about getting older or looking a bit worse for wear, and they look at me like I have two heads. They don't seem to see it at all. 

So, part of my brain says, okay, maybe it's just the lighting in those specific photos, maybe it's just the angle of the camera, maybe I'm making a mountain out of a molehill. But then I go into the bathroom, I look in the mirror, and I see it so clearly. It's right there. The unevenness is just staring back at me. So to answer your question... I guess I know that other people, like my wife and my clients, are telling me it's not really there, or at least that they barely notice it, but when I look at myself, especially after seeing those family photos, it feels completely real to me. It's just so incredibly hard to reconcile what I'm seeing with my own two eyes with what everyone else is saying, and that's why my mind just keeps spinning its wheels on it all day long.
Do you think about your jawline when you're alone and not looking in a mirror?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, it doesn't just turn off when I walk away from the glass. It's... it's almost like a background noise that's always playing, you know? Like, even if I'm just sitting in my office alone, reviewing a portfolio or looking at the market data, I can almost physically feel the heaviness on that side of my face. It's always on my mind, and it really drives this whole routine I've developed. 

Like, before client meetings—and I have a lot of them, obviously, being a financial advisor—I don't just walk straight into the conference room anymore. I can't. I'll go to the restroom first, and I'll check the bathroom mirror. But the lighting in our office bathrooms is that really harsh, overhead fluorescent kind, so I'll actually pull out my phone camera and check it on there several times, just sort of toggling between the screen and the mirror. I'll spend God knows how long in there trying to adjust the lighting, or I'll mess with my shirt, maybe change how my collar sits to see if it casts a better shadow that hides the unevenness. I'll practice angling my face just right, tilting my chin up or turning slightly to the right, so the drooping isn't as obvious when I finally walk into the room. 

And then, to get back to your question about when I'm not looking in a mirror... when I'm actually out there in the meeting, my mind is still completely stuck on it. Because instead of actually focusing on the conversation I'm supposed to be having, I catch myself constantly comparing my face to everyone else's. I'll look at the younger advisors at the firm—these guys right out of business school with these sharp, perfect jawlines—or I'll be thinking about the people at those gallery events I mentioned earlier, and I'm just sitting there analyzing their faces, comparing their bone structure to mine. I'll be nodding along, pretending to listen to a client's retirement goals, but internally, I'm just obsessing over how my jaw doesn't look like theirs. So, yeah, even without a mirror in front of me, I'm still completely wrapped up in it.
Does your concern about your jawline ever shift to other parts of your face or body, or is it always focused on the jawline?

No, it’s... well, honestly, no. It really doesn't shift around. It is always just the jawline. I mean, I’m forty-five, so it’s not like I’m under some illusion that I’m supposed to look like I did when I was twenty-two, right? I’ve got some gray coming in at the temples, a few lines around my eyes, and... and I’m actually completely fine with all of that. In fact, in my line of work, looking a little older, having a bit of salt and pepper, it actually helps. It gives you some gravitas, you know? Clients want to trust their life savings to someone who looks like they’ve been around the block a few times, not some kid fresh out of undergrad. 

So I don't worry about my hair, or my nose, or my weight... I try to hit the gym a couple of times a week, keep myself in decent shape, and I’m perfectly content with the rest of my body. It is literally just this one specific thing. It always comes back to the jaw. Always that one side, always that sagging, pulling look I was telling you about. It’s like... it’s like my brain just puts blinders on to everything else. I could be wearing a brand new, perfectly tailored suit for a big pitch that usually makes me feel like a million bucks, but the second I catch my reflection, none of that matters. My eyes just immediately zero in on that drooping on the lower half of my face, and the rest of me just sort of fades out. 

It’s incredibly frustrating, honestly, because if it weren't for that one specific area, I really think I’d be completely fine with how I look. I wouldn't be spending all this time in the bathroom adjusting my collar or trying to find the right shadow. But because that unevenness is just so prominent to me, it just anchors all my attention right there, all day long. So, no, it never really jumps to my nose or my skin or anything else. It's just this one relentless thing with the jaw.
Has your concern about your jawline led to any significant changes in your daily routine or habits?

Well, it’s not like I’ve stopped working or anything dramatic like that. I mean, I still get through my day, I still manage my portfolios, and I still handle my clients. I haven't let my business completely fall apart. But... yes, it has definitely changed things. It slows me down a lot, especially in the mornings or right before an appointment. 

Getting out the door for client meetings has become this whole exhausting ordeal. Like I was saying before about the bathroom checks, it’s never just a quick glance on the way out anymore. I’ll be packing up my briefcase, looking at the clock, knowing I need to leave to beat the traffic or get to the conference room on time, but I just feel this overwhelming pull to go back to the mirror one more time. I’ll stand there, shifting my jaw, trying to see if it looks as bad as I think it does, messing with my tie, pulling at my collar to see if I can hide it. And before I know it, ten, fifteen minutes have gone by, and I’m rushing, getting stressed out, which probably just makes me look worse anyway. 

And then, when I finally get to the meeting... I’m just not all there. I'm significantly less present during the appointments. A client will be sitting across from me, pouring their heart out about their retirement dreams or worrying about their kids' college funds, and I’m nodding, making eye contact, saying all the right things... but in my head? In my head, I’m just wondering if they’re staring at the sag on the side of my face. I’m completely distracted. I’m supposed to be this sharp, attentive financial advisor that they can trust with their life savings, but half my brain is just totally occupied with my jawline. 

And it's not just work, either. Outside the office, it’s started bleeding into my social life. My wife and I, we usually go to these gallery events—I think I mentioned the art openings earlier. It’s great networking, we know a lot of the local artists, and we genuinely used to enjoy it. But lately... I’ve actually skipped a few of them. I just couldn't bring myself to go. The thought of being in those bright, harsh gallery lights, standing around with all these well-dressed people... and the cameras. There’s always someone taking photos for the gallery’s social media or a local magazine, and after what happened with those family photos I told you about, I just... I can’t stand the thought of being photographed. I panic at the idea of seeing another picture of my face looking all lopsided. So I make up an excuse, I tell my wife I’m too drained from the market closing or that I have a headache, and I just stay home. So, I guess, yeah... I’m still functioning, but it’s definitely changing how I live my life, and it’s just exhausting.
Is there anything that could make you feel like your jawline looks perfectly fine?

I... gosh, I don’t know. I mean, I really don't think there is. And believe me, I have spent an embarrassing amount of time trying to find something, anything, that would just give me some peace of mind about it. I’ve tried to manufacture situations where it looks okay. Like, I’ll go into the guest bedroom downstairs—because the window in there faces east, and the morning light is a lot softer, a lot more diffused than the harsh bulbs in our master bath—and I’ll stand there, and for a split second, I might think, "Okay, maybe it’s not so bad today. Maybe I’m just overthinking it." But it never lasts. I’ll turn my head even just a fraction of an inch to check, or I’ll swallow, or the sun will shift behind a cloud, and boom, the illusion is completely gone and I see that sagging all over again. 

And it’s not like I haven’t tried to listen to other people, either. My wife, she is incredibly supportive. We’ve been married fifteen years, and she’ll see me stressing out before a dinner party or something, and she’ll tell me I look handsome. She’ll say, "Honey, you look great, absolutely nobody is looking at your jaw, I promise." And I desperately want to believe her. I’ll sit there in the car on the way to the restaurant, just repeating what she said in my head, trying to let it be enough. But it just isn't. Because I know she loves me, so of course she’s going to say that, right? She’s biased. 

I’ve even caught myself late at night—after she’s gone to bed—just sitting in the den with my iPad, scrolling through articles about, I don't know, cosmetic things. Fillers, skin tightening, all those procedures they market to guys my age now. But then I go down this whole rabbit hole reading about them, and I start thinking, what if they mess it up? What if they make it look worse, or completely unnatural? And honestly, even if I did something like that, I don't even know if my brain would let me see it as fixed. I feel like my eyes are just permanently trained to find the flaw now. 

So... no. I really don't think there's a magic lighting, or a perfect angle, or anything anyone could say that would make me look in the mirror and think it looks perfectly fine. The doubt always just rushes right back in before I can even step away from the glass.
Is your concern about your jawline something that you think could potentially be fixed or improved with some kind of treatment or intervention?

I... well, I really don't know. I honestly don't. Like I was just mentioning with the late-night iPad scrolling, I see all these ads and articles now. It almost seems like the internet knows I'm worried about it, because every time I open up a news site or even check my professional networks, there's some sponsored post about, you know, non-surgical jawline contouring for men, or injections, or these radio-frequency skin tightening machines. And part of me thinks, well, maybe? Maybe one of those could just tighten that one specific side up, just enough to even it out and make it match the other side. 

But then... then the reality of it sets in, and I start spiraling. I mean, what if I go in for something like that, and they overdo it? You see these guys sometimes, even just guys around the golf course or at the firm, who clearly had some "work" done, and they look... they look like mannequins. It looks so unnatural. And in my profession, trust and stability are absolutely everything. If I show up to a quarterly review meeting and my face looks completely different, or swollen, or unnaturally sharp, my clients are going to notice. They’re going to sit there wondering why the guy managing their retirement funds is suddenly getting cosmetic procedures, you know? It sends the completely wrong message. It might make them think I'm vain, or distracted, or having some sort of midlife crisis, and I absolutely cannot afford to project that kind of image.

So, I don't know if it can be fixed. Because even if there was a perfect procedure out there—one that was completely undetectable and just magically lifted that one sagging spot—I still come back to what I was saying a minute ago. Would my brain even let me see it as fixed? Or would I just stand in front of the mirror, in that harsh master bathroom light, and find a new shadow? Or convince myself that the injection is lumpy, or that the other side is starting to sag now? It’s like... I desperately want to believe there’s a physical fix, a doctor out there who could just do a quick treatment and make me feel normal again, but I’m terrified of making it worse. And honestly, I'm even more terrified that the problem is just permanently wired into how my eyes are processing my reflection now. So I just stay stuck in this miserable limbo. I research, I read the reviews, I look at before-and-after photos for hours on end... and then I close the browser and do absolutely nothing, because I just don't have a real answer.
Do you think it's possible that the unevenness you see in your jawline is something that only you can see?

Well, I mean... logically, I hear what you're asking. And if you were to ask the people around me, they would probably agree with that theory. Because, like I was saying about my wife, she says she barely notices anything. And I’ve even sort of... well, I've fished for reassurance a bit with a couple of my really long-term clients. People I’ve managed money for over a decade, where we have a pretty comfortable, friendly rapport. I'll make a self-deprecating joke about getting older or my face falling, and they just look at me like I’m speaking a different language. They swear they don't see what I'm talking about. 

But... see, what brings me in here, what I just can't seem to get past, is that I keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and that one side of my face. It is just so glaringly obvious to me. Especially—and I know I brought this up earlier, but it really was the catalyst for all of this—especially after seeing myself in all those family photos. 

We had hired a professional photographer last fall because my wife wanted these really nice, outdoor portraits for our holiday cards. We went to this park, the leaves were changing, the whole nine yards. And when the photographer emailed us the gallery of digital proofs a couple of weeks later... I was just horrified. I clicked on the very first picture, zoomed in on my face, and there it was. That lopsided, sagging jowl area. It was just staring right back at me in high definition. I ended up spending hours, literally hours that evening, going through all seventy-something proofs, just analyzing the angle of my jaw in every single shot. My wife was trying to pick out which ones to print for the grandparents, and I was just completely fixated on this one side of my face looking like it was practically melting off my skull. 

So, to answer your question... I know my wife and my clients say they barely notice anything, and maybe they really don't. Maybe people just don't look at us as closely as we look at ourselves. But the camera caught it. The camera lens doesn't lie, right? It captured exactly what I see in the mirror. So even if other people are just being polite, or if they're just too wrapped up in their own lives to notice my flaws... I know it's there. I have photographic proof of it. And once you see something like that in a high-resolution photo, you just... you can't unsee it. I just can't get it out of my head, no matter how many times someone tells me it's fine.
Do you think it's possible that the unevenness you perceive in your jawline is not visible to others because it doesn't actually exist, rather than just because they're not noticing it?

I... wow. That is... that's really hard to even process. To say it doesn't exist at all? I just don't know how I could possibly accept that. Because, I mean, I see it. I see it every single day. I see the physical droop, the way the skin folds differently on that one side compared to the other. 

When I'm shaving in the morning—and this is something I deal with every single day—I can literally feel the difference in the contour with my razor. I actually have to tilt my neck at a completely different angle on that side, pull the skin a little tighter, just to get a clean shave without nicking myself because the jawline isn't as sharp there. It's softer, it's sagging. So, if we're saying it doesn't exist... it makes me feel like I'm completely losing my grip on reality, you know? 

And as a financial advisor, my entire career, my entire life really, is built on objective reality. Numbers, spreadsheets, market trends... things you can prove. You look at a ledger, and the deficit is either there or it isn't. You can't just pretend a bad investment doesn't exist because you don't want to look at it. So when I look at those family photos, or when I'm standing in the bathroom under those awful LED lights, I feel like I am looking at a deficit. I'm looking at a physical reality. 

I mean, I suppose theoretically, I know the human brain is capable of playing tricks on people, right? You read about that stuff, how people's minds can distort things. But this isn't some sort of hallucination. It's a structural unevenness. It feels like it's just gravity and aging hitting one side of my face significantly harder than the other. 

So... no, I just can't wrap my head around the idea that it simply isn't there. If it wasn't there, why would I have to adjust how I shave? Why would I be spending hours analyzing those digital proofs from the photographer? Why would I be losing sleep over it, sitting in the dark with my iPad researching skin tightening? It has to be real. It has to be. Even if it's just... maybe it's just really subtle to everyone else because they aren't staring at it up close, but to me, it's monumental. It's right there on my face.
Do you think it's possible that your jawline actually looks normal to everyone else, but you're the only one who sees it as uneven?

I mean... I guess I have to concede that it's a possibility, right? If I'm being completely objective and looking at the data, I know I keep bringing this same point up, but the evidence from the people around me points in that direction. Like I said, my wife and those long-term clients... they swear they barely notice anything at all. They act like I'm making a mountain out of a molehill. So, yes, maybe to the rest of the world, it just looks like a normal forty-five-year-old guy's face. 

But... and this is exactly what brings me in to see you today, because I just can't keep living with this mental weight... I keep getting completely stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jawline. It's that one specific side of my face. And I know I've already talked your ear off about those family photos we took last fall, but I really can't overstate how much of a turning point that was for me. Before that, maybe it was just a passing thought, but seeing those high-resolution proofs... it just locked it in for me. 

Because even if my wife is telling the truth, even if my clients truly, genuinely don't see it and think I look perfectly fine... I see it. I'm the one who has to live inside this head. I'm the one sitting in a conference room trying to explain a complex Roth IRA conversion to a couple, and half my brain is just totally distracted, wondering if the lighting in the room is casting a shadow on my jowl. I just can't stop picturing those digital proofs from the photographer. So whether my jawline actually looks normal to everyone else or not almost feels beside the point now, because I'm the one who is completely, utterly preoccupied with it every waking minute. It's just exhausting, honestly. I can't turn it off.
Do you think it's possible that your jawline looks perfectly normal, but your mind is distorting your perception of it?

Distorting... I mean, you're asking if my brain is just, what, putting a funhouse mirror over my eyes? 

Look, I know I sound like a broken record today. I know I keep circling back to the exact same things, but there's a reason for that. What actually brings me in here—the whole reason I finally picked up the phone to make this appointment—is that I just keep getting completely stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and that one side of my face. I cannot let it go. 

I know I've already harped on those family photos we took in the park, and I know I've told you multiple times now that my wife and my clients say they barely notice anything at all. I hear myself saying it. But even if I try to entertain this idea that my mind is playing some massive trick on me, or distorting the image... the reality is that the preoccupation is completely taking over my life. 

It’s like I’m trapped in this mental loop. I try to rationalize it. I try to tell myself, "Hey, your wife says you look fine, your clients don't care, just drop it." But then I catch my reflection in the window of my office, or I'm trying to read the Wall Street Journal over my morning coffee, and boom, my brain just snaps right back to that lopsided jowl. I'm right back to zooming in on those digital proofs in my head. 

So, I don't know. Is it possible my perception is distorted? Maybe? I don't have a psychology degree, I just did some college before jumping into finance. But whatever my brain is doing, whether it's a distortion or not, the result is the same. I am just entirely fixated on this unevenness, and I can't seem to unsee it or think about anything else, no matter how much logic I try to apply to it.
Do you think it's possible that your jawline looks perfectly normal to everyone, including in photographs, but you're the only one who perceives it as uneven?

I mean, we are really beating this drum today, aren't we? Look, I get what you're trying to ask. You're asking if the actual physical photographs—the raw data, so to speak—look completely fine to the rest of the world, and I'm just the lone holdout who sees a disaster. 

And... well, maybe? I guess? But honestly, doc, like I keep trying to explain, what actually brings me in here, the whole crux of the issue, is that I just keep getting incredibly, undeniably stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and that one side of my face. I just can't move past it. Especially—and I know I've brought this up like five times already, but it's just so central to all of this—especially after seeing myself in all those family photos from the park.
